subject: anaesthesia
title: Resuscitation: Basic Life Support, Defibrillation, and Capnography in CPR

steps.title: High-Quality Chest Compressions
steps.tx: **High-quality chest compression metrics** form the foundation of successful cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) according to International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) guidelines: compress the lower half of the sternum to a depth of 5 to 6 centimeters (2 to 2.4 inches) in adults, maintain a compression rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute, allow complete chest wall recoil between compressions, and minimize hands-off interruptions to under 10 seconds.

steps.title: Compression-to-Ventilation Ratios
steps.tx: **Standard CPR compression-ventilation ratios** dictate a 30:2 ratio (30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths) for single rescuers across adults, children, and infants. For healthcare providers executing two-rescuer CPR in children and infants, the ratio shifts to 15:2 to prioritize higher ventilatory demands. Once an advanced endotracheal airway is secured, deliver continuous chest compressions with one asynchronous breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute).

steps.title: Defibrillation Shockable versus Non-Shockable
steps.tx: **Cardiac arrest rhythm stratification** divides into shockable rhythms (ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia) and non-shockable rhythms (asystole and pulseless electrical activity). Shockable rhythms require immediate defibrillation with a single shock of 120 to 200 Joules for biphasic waveforms (or 360 Joules for monophasic), immediately followed by two minutes of uninterrupted CPR before rhythm re-checking.

left.title: Shockable Rhythms (VF / Pulseless VT)
points: Chaotic ventricular fibrillation or broad-complex pulseless VT
Immediate defibrillation with 120 to 200 Joules biphasic energy
Administer amiodarone (300 mg) after the third shock

right.title: Non-Shockable Rhythms (Asystole / PEA)
points: Flatline asystole or organized rhythm without palpable pulse
Defibrillation is completely ineffective and contraindicated
Administer IV adrenaline (1 mg) immediately; hunt for reversible causes

steps.title: Adrenaline and Amiodarone Dosing
steps.tx: **Pharmacotherapy algorithms in cardiac arrest** dictate administering intravenous adrenaline (1 milligram of 1:10,000 solution) every 3 to 5 minutes: given immediately in non-shockable rhythms, or after the second defibrillation shock in shockable rhythms. For refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia persisting after the third shock, administer intravenous amiodarone at 300 milligrams (with a second dose of 150 mg after the fifth shock), or lidocaine (1 to 1.5 mg/kg).

steps.title: Reversible Causes: 4 Hs and 4 Ts
steps.tx: **Reversible causes of cardiac arrest** must be methodically identified and corrected during CPR cycles, categorized into the 4 Hs: Hypoxia (ventilate 100% O2), Hypovolaemia (rapid fluid/blood bolus), Hypothermia (active warming), and Hyper/Hypokalaemia and metabolic disorders. The 4 Ts comprise: Tension pneumothorax (needle decompression), cardiac Tamponade (pericardiocentesis), Toxins (antidotes), and Thrombosis (pulmonary embolus or coronary thrombosis).

steps.title: Capnography as a Quality Indicator
steps.tx: **End-tidal carbon dioxide monitoring during CPR** serves as an objective real-time indicator of resuscitation quality and cardiac output. An EtCO2 under 10 mmHg indicates inadequate chest compression depth or fatigue, demanding immediate improvement in compression technique. An EtCO2 consistently between 15 and 20 mmHg confirms high-quality CPR generating adequate pulmonary blood flow.

left.title: EtCO2 Under 10 mmHg
points: Inadequate chest compression depth or improper hand placement
Rescuer physical exhaustion or severe systemic hypoperfusion
Predicts zero chance of survival if persistent for 20 minutes

right.title: EtCO2 Greater than 15 to 20 mmHg
points: Generates sufficient pulmonary blood flow to transport CO2
Associated with significantly improved resuscitation survival

steps.title: Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC)
steps.tx: **Capnographic sign of return of spontaneous circulation** is a sudden, dramatic jump in end-tidal carbon dioxide to 35 to 45 mmHg or higher. This abrupt surge occurs because restored spontaneous cardiac output instantly delivers accumulated metabolic carbon dioxide from peripheral tissues to the pulmonary circulation, providing an early sign of ROSC without needing to pause chest compressions for pulse palpation.

nodes.label: CPR in progress with baseline EtCO2 of 15 mmHg
Sudden massive surge of EtCO2 jumping to 35 to 45 mmHg
Halt compressions, palpate carotid pulse, and initiate post-resuscitation care

steps.tx: For minutes the capnogram has been reporting the quality of compressions, low and steady, when suddenly it leaps towards forty. That abrupt **EtCO2 jump** means a spontaneous heart has taken over, washing accumulated carbon dioxide from the tissues into the lungs in one surge. The team learns of ROSC from the trace without pausing compressions to hunt for a pulse. A gradual climb can warn of improving compression quality too, making this waveform a coach during the arrest and a herald at its end.
steps.say: A sudden EtCO2 jump to around forty signals return of spontaneous circulation without stopping compressions.

steps.title: Targeted Temperature Management Post-ROSC
steps.tx: **Post-cardiac arrest targeted temperature management** (TTM) prevents secondary ischemic reperfusion brain injury in comatose adult patients following ROSC. Current guidelines mandate maintaining a constant core temperature strictly between 32 and 36 degrees Celsius for at least 24 hours using surface cooling blankets or intravascular catheters, actively preventing fever (temperature above 37.7C) for 72 hours.
